title: US lawmakers call for UK court to lift secrecy over Apple ‘backdoor’ surveillance
raw_text:
US lawmakers are urging a UK court to lift the secrecy around UK government moves to require Apple to create a “back door” into its end-to-end encrypted data storage, ahead of a court hearing next week.

In a letter to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, US Democratic senator, Ron Wyden, and Republican Warren Davidson, warned that the UK’s unprecedented secrecy is needlessly straining the relations between the two countries.

The letter comes ahead of a case management hearing by the Investigatory Powers Tribunal that will consider a new complaint by Apple against the Home Office over a secret order to give the UK access to end-to-end encrypted messages, photographs and data stored on Apple’s iCloud service.

The letter reveals that Apple has sought permission from the UK government to discuss the order with the executive and legislative branches of the US government. Apple has been given permission to brief the US Attorney General, the Vice President, and their staff, but has been explicitly prohibited from discussing the matter with the US Congress.

Weakening encryption poses security risks

“Weakening encryption in consumer software introduces critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited by hostile foreign actors,” the lawmakers wrote. “Congress cannot fulfill its constitutional duty to evaluate and mitigate these national security threats if foreign non-disclosure orders are weaponized to prevent US technology companies from answering inquiries from duly elected lawmakers.”

The congressmen state that under the US system, Congress is not only a co-equal branch of government, it is the “First Branch of the US government”. It is “wholly inappropriate” for the UK to attempt to dictate the distribution of powers within the US government, they write.

The UK first issued a secret order to require Apple to provide the capability for the UK to access end-to-end encrypted phone messages, photographs and data of users worldwide, including US citizens, from Apple’s iCloud service, in January 2025, leaks to the Washington Post revealed.

US pushback led to UK rethink

The US government pushed back, when Wyden and republican representative Andy Biggs urged the then US Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Tulsi Gabbard, to remove the UK from the 65-year-old UK-USA signals intelligence sharing agreement, if the UK did not withdraw its order against Apple.

Gabbard warned that the UK’s surveillance demands, which would weaken the security and encryption of American citizens, would be a “clear and egregious violation of Americans’ privacy and civil liberties”.

The outcry appears to have persuaded the UK to withdraw its first order against Apple, bringing a temporary end to Apple’s legal proceedings against the Home Office in the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

The Home Office went on to issue a new order against Apple, in October 2025, which restricted UK access to the end-to-end encrypted data of UK citizens stored on the iCloud.

Full scope of UK order unknown

However, according to Wyden and Davidson, the full scope of the current request is unknown, both to the public and members of Congress, because of secrecy mandated by the UK government.

The lawmakers urge the UK’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal to consider the “profound constitutional and intergovernmental implications” of Technical Capability Notices served on technology companies.

They call for “open justice” in the tribunal, which frequently holds hearings in closed session, to allow independent cyber security experts and impacted stakeholders to evaluate the technical demands of the order against Apple.

“The Tribunal should ensure that no surveillance demand issued under UK law is permitted to restrict U.S. companies from fully informing and engaging with the United States Congress,” the letter states.

The order, known as a Technical Capability Notice, targets users of Apple’s Advanced Data Protection (ADP). The optional service allows Apple customers to encrypt data and messages stored on iCloud with their own encryption keys, making it impossible for Apple or anyone else without access to those keys to decrypt and read the stored data.

Apple withdrew its ADP service from the UK in February 2025, stating, “As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”

The campaign groups Privacy International and Liberty, together with two individual users of ADP, are bringing a separate legal challenge against the Home Office, which is expected to be joined to Apple’s legal challenge, in a hearing on 17 September 2026.

title: UK government to create team to validate Capita’s data on troubled pension scheme
raw_text:

Capita has denied claims made in a Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) member forum that it could be years before the service meets expected standards, calling it “opinion” rather than “fact”.

Since it took over the contract from previous supplier MyCSP in December 2025, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises and left claimants in severe financial difficulties, including months with no income.

According to the government department’s director in charge of the scheme, the process of creating a team that will have direct access to Capita systems to check that data provided by the outsourcer is reliable.

Unwanted reliance

In an email exchange with a CSPS member, scheme director Richard Vianello admitted the government is “currently reliant on management information provided by Capita”, but said he is “looking to change that”.

The CSPS claimant wrote that the government should stop relying on Capita’s figures. “It’s not an exemption to quote them without checking their veracity,” they said. “A cabinet office or independent person should be in there who can provide genuine data.”

The process to do this has begun, Vianello told the CSPS claimant. “… We are in the process of sifting applications for a new Quality Assurance function in One Gov/Cabinet Office,” he wrote. “I have agreed with Capita that this team will have direct access to Capita systems, and be able to validate/assure the data we receive.”

He added that the government is already “delving into the information provided and selecting cases at random for a quality assurance walkthrough” and has asked independent remedial advisor Grant Thornton to review a sample of cases.

“Following feedback from members, I have committed to providing data going forward on the oldest cases, where the member or administrator has been waiting over 100 days,” said Vianello. “My aim is to provide this data consistently, so members can see progress over time. In previous updates we have shared different aspects of delivery, and I agree that it has been difficult to unpick progress as a result.”

The Cabinet Office said it is “continuing to build capability in its management team to ensure continued strong oversight, including on data”.

Overdue payments

The email exchange began with the CSPS member bringing to Vianello’s attention claims being made on the CSPS member Facebook page that it could be years before the Capita service reaches the quality expected.

Members of the CSPS scheme have contacted Computer Weekly and are deeply concerned about the allegations.

The claims, said to be from a conversation with a scheme member and the CSPS helpline, were published on a member group forum, and have been sent to Computer Weekly by two people independently.

The claims included that there were between 130,000 and 140,000 outstanding overdue payments waiting to be issued for people that have already had claims approved. Another, that it will take many months or even years for Capita to bring the delivery of their service in line with the service level agreement and the person making the claim, raised doubts that they will ever be able to do so.

“If true, this is a huge concern,” said one CSPS member still waiting for his pension.

In reply to the member, Vianello wrote: “I do not recognise the data that has apparently been shared.”

In response to the claim, Capita said: “As you must accept, our brilliant and hardworking helpline colleagues are not party to the full detail of the remediation plan. If this exchange did take place as you described, the anonymous Capita team member would have been expressing an opinion, rather than a fact.”

The Cabinet Office says it does not recognise the overdue figures quoted.

Capita won the CSPS administration contract in 2023, when the Cabinet Office awarded Capita a seven-year deal worth £239m. It was set to replace MyCSP on 1 December 2025, but it has seen huge disruption and chaos for members since then.

Trouble from go

Early, in October last year, a couple of months before Capita was set to take over, a Public Accounts Committee (PAC) report said there is a “real risk” that Capita will not be ready to take over the administration of the scheme on time. The outsourcer hit back, claiming it is “not reflective of the current state of the transition”, calling the report inaccurate.

There have been multiple PAC hearings since, featuring both Capita and the Cabinet Office, with reassurances repeatedly given to MPs that Capita would get the service to the expected levels.

Capita said: “We recognise there is more to do to restore the service members should expect. Our focus remains on resolving outstanding cases and delivering against the next milestone in the remediation plan at the end of September.

“We remain sorry for the impact the service issues have had on members and are continuing to work closely with the Cabinet Office as we deliver the wider recovery.”

The scheme looks set to be brought in-house, but such a move would be in line with the government’s plan to “move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation”.

A Cabinet Office Spokesperson said: “The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable. Our immediate priority is to stabilise the service to give current and former Civil Servants the service they deserve.

“While robust commercial levers will continue to be applied in the short term, including withholding nearly £10m in payments, the government intends to move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation and is actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house.”

title: GDPR wasn't designed for AI and that's a security problem
raw_text:
When the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) came into force, generative AI wasn’t embedded in everyday business applications, AI agents were not executing multi-step tasks across corporate databases and prompt injection was not a mainstream vector for data exfiltration.

GDPR is one of the world's most important pieces of data protection legislation and its principles are highly relevant to AI. But it was designed around a very different data environment. AI has introduced fundamentally different ways for data to be processed, inferred, retrieved and exposed, introducing challenges and compliance risks that could not have been anticipated.

This doesn’t mean GDPR has become obsolete, but we do need to question whether the way organisations demonstrate compliance is enough when the systems processing personal data can themselves be manipulated.  Take prompt injection. An organisation may have strong access controls around a database containing sensitive customer information, and a clearly documented lawful basis for processing and robust policies around retention and deletion. But if it gives an AI assistant access to that database, an attacker could manipulate the AI into retrieving information that it has legitimate access to.

The underlying data controls may be working but the vulnerability exists in the layer between the user, the AI and the systems it can access. One of the important differences AI introduces is that security is not just about preventing unauthorised access; it is also about preventing authorised AI systems from being manipulated into producing illegal outcomes.

This risk escalates exponentially as enterprises deploy agentic workflows. An AI agent may be able to search internal documents, send emails, update records, access customer systems or interact with other applications. Every additional capability creates another potential route to personal data if the agent can be manipulated.

When it comes to AI, are documented controls, a data protection impact assessment and appropriate policies enough to demonstrate GDPR compliance? Or should organisations also be able to demonstrate that they have actively tested the system?  GDPR requires that organisations implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data. However, in an AI environment, those measures can’t be assessed just by looking at whether they exist. Organisations need to understand how they perform when an AI system is subjected to adversarial conditions.

  • Advisory guidelines clarifying when organisations can scrape and reuse personal data to build GenAI models are among a raft of announcements at the inaugural Singapore Data Festival.
  • As part of a legal settlement over its child safety measures, Meta will have to pay $18bn over a 10-year period, and implement a number of changes to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.

That means testing for prompt injection and data leakage, examining what an AI system can reveal through carefully constructed interactions and determining whether an agent can be manipulated into accessing or transmitting information outside its intended purpose. It also means testing the permissions given to AI systems and considering what happens when those permissions are abused.

AI therefore needs to be treated as part of the attack surface, not as an application that can be assessed once and then considered secure. AI systems behave differently from conventional applications, with outputs influenced by inputs, context and interactions. A system that appears secure under normal conditions may behave differently when confronted with an adversarial interaction.

A compliance assessment carried out when an AI system is deployed cannot necessarily tell an organisation how that system will behave several months later, after the underlying model has changed, new data sources have been connected or its permissions have expanded. GDPR compliance in an AI environment therefore needs to be continuous rather than static.

There is also a capability challenge. Developers need to understand the security implications of the AI systems they build, while security professionals need hands-on experience defending against adversarial AI techniques. Crucially, organisations must evaluate human-AI readiness, proving that human operators have the technical dexterity to direct, validate, and override autonomous agents when they hallucinate or fall under attack. That knowledge cannot come solely from policies or theoretical training. Teams need opportunities to test these scenarios in realistic conditions and understand how systems behave when those attacks succeed.

AI provides another route where personal data can be exposed and having a policy stating that an AI system must protect personal data is not enough. Organisations need to be able to demonstrate that the system has been tested, its permissions challenged and potential routes to data exposure investigated, alongside having people with the capability to respond when something goes wrong.

GDPR’s principles around privacy, accountability, data minimisation and security are arguably even more important with AI. But the regulation can’t have anticipated every mechanism through which AI can expose personal information and organisations cannot rely on compliance approaches developed for a fundamentally different technological environment.

The future of GDPR compliance will need more than governance and documentation. It will need evidence that organisations have actively tested their AI systems, challenged their assumptions and assessed how those systems behave under attack. It will also need evidence that the people responsible for building and defending them have the practical capabilities to identify and respond to emerging threats.

title: IT event dive: Through the AWS public sector symposium revolving door
raw_text:
It’s a sunny morning in the City of London, and I’m off to the AWS Public Sector AI Symposium. From my hotel room, one end of Tower Bridge peeps through the gaps in nondescript office blocks. Crystal Palace Hill sits distant, and a railway line runs; less used than I expected it to be when I first spotted it. But it’s Fenchurch Street, so that figures.

It is early autumn, just into September, and there is still damp on the rooftops from earlier rain. I check out of the hotel through a plush-but-unstylish lounge and out past the Princess of Prussia. It’s the kind of pub that looks like one I would want to drink in, though I don’t stop to find out whether it really does sell the stouts, mild ales and porter its century-old ceramic frontage suggests.

The streets are cool and full of traffic; off towards Aldgate, vehicles moving at a crawl next to me, pretty much walking pace. F&M men smoke outside a building. There’s a Tesco Express, city workers off to work, and blocks of public housing nestling where one would least expect.

Opposite the social housing, it’s a mix of actual old buildings and 90s fake marble-fronted offices. One of them is the now-defunct Sungard Availability Services, which wears a rounded, perspex-fronted lift but is absolutely covered in graffiti anywhere in human reach – looks like it might not be too available anymore.

On past hoardings plastered with posters: “Drum and Bass Weekender”, “You and Me Comedy”, “Dub Vendor”.

Past the dragon-on-a-plinth marker of the City of London boundary, and past St Botolph Without Aldgate – the city belying its older existence. There is even a bingo hall, not something you expect to find in the city, though I suppose many here play bingo all day long in some sense.

Our venue is 133 Houndsditch, and I nearly walk straight past, then turn to see it. In through the main entrance and a revolving door, then helpful staff, one of whom says “prass” instead of “press” in the way young home counties folk seem to these days. My e-ticket loads easily from email. Up to the second floor, where the event is happening, and I am early.

Croissants and listening walls

Rows of tables hold miniature croissants (pictured), smoothies and juice. Partner stands line the walls. One firm, Version1, uses artificial intelligence (AI) to listen to an entire room’s conversations to surface IT solutions in near to real time – like a useful version of everybody’s paranoid ideas about mobile phones that eavesdrop. An Indian man from PA Consulting explains the messy business of migrating large public sector organisations. But it’s time to get to work.

I am in my red-striped 1970/80s Van Heusen shirt, still awaiting my Amazon Web Service (AWS) press office guide, and I duck out of forced conversations to take my press seat in front of the stage. 

A data scientist from King’s College London plonks down beside me and introduces herself. My use of large language models (LLMs) in code editors has changed my work in data journalism significantly in recent times, and I’m keen to talk, especially to a “real” data scientist – I’m self-taught.

Meanwhile, the session is due to start. IT event favourite Daft Punk ramps up over the PA. No dry ice, though. It doesn’t feel like a rave at 9am, which is a nice change from many vendor events.

Revolving doors everywhere

The building entrance, it turns out, was not the only revolving door. The keynote opens with the host, AWS’s Holly Ellis, a veteran of a number of government posts including the Home Office. By late-morning I’ve lost count of the AWS and supplier speakers that reference their public sector past lives.

AWS’s David Appel opens by talking about the 1951 Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace, “a million square feet of glass and iron built in just nine months”, and a pitch that references the high water mark of British Empire industry and capitalism, and the parallels between electrification and AI. His colleague, Ash Thankey, brings the gush. “We love you guys,” he tells the room. “Thank you, thank you, thank you, from the bottom of our hearts.”

The numbers come thick and fast: 58% of public sector organisations have adopted AI, yet only 31% have reached the advanced stage, and redesigning workflows earns efficiency gains of 68% against 40% for basic users. 

Accenture’s Hacer Evans, a 27-year civil servant until recently, is more prosaic. She talks about “scalers” and warns that leadership, not technology, is the gap.

Social good peeps through

A panel discussion follows. I grimace inwardly at the mention of The Tony Blair Institute, but its representative brings insight, talking of the cost of deprivation that results from the UK as “the third most unequal country in the OECD developed nations”.

Later, Maggie Philbin, former Tomorrow’s World presenter, hands the stage to students Miranda and Safa, who talk about AI literacy, and the soft skills needed for a successful AI future. It’s another moment when the event stops selling and social good comes through.

Afterwards, I am whisked (thanks again to my AWS press office guide) to an interview with Proximie and University Hospital of Coventry and Warwickshire.

It’s lunchtime when I leave. Past registration, into the lift, down to the ground floor. I’ve taken in so much that it feels like an age since I arrived, but it has only been four hours. Information was densely packed; I later found out I’d recorded 30,000 words.

I gather my bearings, go through the revolving door and emerge onto a street full of office workers. I duck through the alleyway to Aldgate Station, past a resting food delivery e-cyclist, enter the arched portal, flash the card at the ticket barrier, and the gates open. That is it.

title: Civil service union welcomes pension scheme insourcing plan
raw_text:
The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) has welcomed the government’s stance on bringing the civil service pension scheme (CSPS) administration in-house.

Plans to bring the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) administration in-house, amid the current problems under the stewardship of outsourcer Capita, are currently being worked on.

PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote met with Sally Jameson MP, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, yesterday (10 September), to discuss the government’s plans to rescue a failed outsourcing contract that has left retirees in financial hardship.

In July, the PCS demanded that the £239m contract to administer about 1.7 million pensions be brought in-house.

Since it took over the contract from previous supplier MyCSP in December 2025, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises, and left claimants in severe financial difficulties. The company has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on Capita, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

Heathcote told Computer Weekly: “I met with Sally Jameson MP yesterday to discuss the ongoing problems with Capita and it was a positive meeting. The minister confirmed that the government is looking seriously at bringing the service back in-house, something PCS has been calling for throughout this crisis.”

A Cabinet Office spokesperson told Computer Weekly previously that the government was “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house”.

Jameson reconfirmed this in a statement to Parliament yesterday.

Inconclusive promise

Despite the seemingly unambiguous statement about the “long-term strategy to bring [CSPS] back in-house”, Heathcote said: “There is still work to do before a final decision is made, but I made clear that PCS wants to be fully involved and kept updated as this develops.

“Public services, including our pensions, should be delivered by properly resourced public servants, not outsourced for private profit,” she added. 

“Capita’s failures have caused far too much stress and uncertainty for our members. Today’s meeting was a positive step, but we’ll keep the pressure on until we have a pensions service that people can rely on.”

Capita has a huge UK public sector client base. According to figures from Tussell, Capita currently has 199 public sector contracts worth a combined £7.9bn. Despite the CSPS failures, Capita won the Synergy Business Process Services contract in March, which, according to the official tender, has an estimated value of around £959m over 10 years. The contract supports back-office services for the Department for Work and Pensions, the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.

But the government’s proposed biggest wave of insourcing in a generation will put pressure to perform on service providers such as Capita.

The firm set a target to process cases within key performance indicators from 30 September 2026.

Jameson said there will be a “substantive update” next month, following the conclusion of the technical audit and report from remedial adviser Grant Thornton.

‘Not good enough’

Capita said: “In the meantime, our focus remains on working through outstanding cases and improving the service members receive. Despite the progress made, we recognise the service has not been good enough, particularly for members waiting on bereavement, retirement and quotation cases, and we are sorry for the impact this has had on those members.”

There have been multiple PAC hearings since, featuring both Capita and the Cabinet Office, with reassurances repeatedly given to MPs that Capita would get the service to the expected levels.

During a joint PAC and Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (Pacac) hearing in July, Pacac chair Simon Hoare MP reminded Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez and his colleagues of promises made to government during the contracting process. The Cabinet Office was told “that the two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service”, he said. “None of that met neither the novel nor the basic.”

In the meeting, Hoare asked: “Isn’t the stark issue, in essence, a company like Capita has the private parts of HMG [His Majesty’s government] very firmly in its grip?”

title: AWS AI Symposium: Public sector must shape AI, use open source
raw_text:
Public sector leaders can secure artificial intelligence (AI) only by treating security as a fast-moving target, by demanding secure-by-default and interoperable technology, and by leaning on open source to build trust and resilience. They can also use their collective purchasing power to shape the market rather than simply buy from it.

That was the message from two public sector voices on a security panel at this week’s AWS Public Sector AI Symposium in London: Caroline Gorski (pictured, right), director of the Digital Commercial Centre of Excellence (DCCOE), and Laura Gilbert (pictured, left), senior director of AI at the Tony Blair Institute.

The panel focused on a question government leaders keep asking: “How do I deploy AI securely?” The security backdrop came from Jason Gwartz, head of core technology at the AI Security Institute (AISI), a Cabinet Office directorate.

The AISI tests frontier models against simulated corporate networks and pieces of critical national infrastructure that a model must attack end-to-end. Last year, models solved only a handful of steps on ranges it designed with 30 or more. In April, a model completed all 32 steps of one range autonomously for the first time. Gwartz put the doubling time of cyber skills at around five months.

Against that context, Gilbert and Gorski offer two different answers to the security question – one technical, one commercial.

Gilbert, who ran the data science and AI team in Downing Street for four and a half years before joining the Tony Blair Institute, which advises just under 50 governments on using AI for public services, opens not with security, but inequality. Done well, she argued, AI narrows the gap; done badly, it widens it and breeds unrest.

She described the UK as “the third most unequal country in the OECD developed nations”, a position that “costs us somewhere between £35bn and about £70bn a year”. The upside is concrete: “Reducing inequality to the mid-level is predicted to reduce people being imprisoned by about 30%, mental health problems by about 5% and murders by 33%.”

Open source for security

Gilbert’s answer to the IT security question is transparency, in the form of open source. In Downing Street, she “immediately adopted this mantra of radical transparency”, open-sourcing all of the team’s code, and publishing blogs on what they built and why.

For government, argued Gilbert, open source does two things. It cuts cost: “I don’t think that we should be competing with big frontier apps on absolute top-tier technology,” she said. “We need models that are very cheap and that can be run on completely constrained infrastructure for security reasons, that are good enough.”

And, counter-intuitively, it improves security: publishing code invites scrutiny rather than inviting attack. “We never once had anyone manage to hack into anything, but we would give them a prize if they did,” said Gilbert. “If you don’t open source, very often, what you’re doing is leaving a space for the bad actors to come in who might be better funded and more determined. And they will find the hole.”

She made the point about how framing shapes acceptance, with the example of an “AI pharmacist”. Tell people “we’re building an AI pharmacist” and they recoil, said Gilbert, but point out that “in the UK, we kill about 22,000 people every year with bad prescriptions, and it costs about a billion pounds, and we don’t have the manpower to solve that”, and it “sounds like a little bit of a better idea”.

Public sector as leader

Where Gilbert reaches for code, Gorski reaches for contracts. The DCCOE blends commercial, technical and delivery expertise and exists, she said, “to help the government and the public sector to become a more ambitious and more intelligent customer for transformative digital technologies”.

The insight behind her argument is that the public sector is a buyer big enough to set terms. As “probably one of the largest single customers” for many AI services, it should “use more of that power and weight to actually shape the markets, not simply to buy what’s already available”. The Cloud challenge book, launched earlier this year, sets out those issues.

“One of the things that we haven’t necessarily done well across government is understand our purchasing power collectively, and what that frees us to ask for from our suppliers in a much more directive and pointed way,” she said.

In practice, Gorski wants price discounts and opportunities to innovate to reach everywhere, “not just in central government, but also in the devolved authorities and the local government”. She wants “interoperability, portability, removing exit penalties” to be “baked into the way that we engage with our technology partners” – including “failover protocols that might fail over to competitors’ service provision” if a cloud region goes down.

The underlying challenge, said Gorski, is for suppliers to deliver “the underlying capabilities to be secure by default, to be resilient by default, to be transparent by design, and to have public value as their primary objective”.

The two arguments converge in the same place. Gilbert said the decisions made now – “who you allow to have access to your data” – will “fully impact the society that we go forward into, our children go forward into”. Gorski framed it as a duty: “Government’s role in emerging markets is to shape emerging markets. And we have a social responsibility to shape those markets in line with what our society wants us to do.”

Public sector leaders can secure artificial intelligence (AI) only by treating security as a fast-moving target, by demanding secure-by-default and interoperable technology, and by leaning on open source to build trust and resilience. They can also use their collective purchasing power to shape the market rather than simply buy from it.

The panel focused on a question government leaders keep asking: “How do I deploy AI securely?” The security backdrop came from Jason Gwartz, head of core technology at the AI Security Institute (AISI), a Cabinet Office directorate.

title: CW@60: Nobody notices when it works
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

When Amazon first invited me to give a talk, I nearly said no. I was an academic who had spent years reasoning about the hardest problems in distributed systems, and here was a bookstore asking for my time. A database and a server, how hard could it be?

Then I got one look inside and saw engineers doing work years ahead of anything I had seen in the lab or the rest of the industry. There was no textbook for what they were building and no off-the-shelf solution, because no one had operated at that scale before.

I have now been at Amazon for more than two decades, and if you had told me on that first visit I would spend 22 years in one place, I would probably have laughed. The job and the industry around it have changed so quickly that I have had a dozen different careers without ever handing in my badge, which is silver now, to go with what remains of the hair.

What held me was the thing I glimpsed that first day - the chance to solve problems other engineers had not yet imagined, usually out of necessity. There is one I remember vividly.

The wrong foundation

Not long after I joined came my worst day at the bookstore. It was 12 December 2004, the last day to place a Christmas order with free shipping, the busiest day of the busiest week of the year, and a bug in the commercial relational database we depended on took the site down for roughly 12 hours.

Half a day without orders was bad enough. What weighed heaviest was the thought of the holidays we had ruined for customers who trusted us to deliver.

The conventional response to our outage would have been to buy a bigger database, which would not have touched the real problem. We were leaning on a relational database as a foundational building block it was never designed to be. When we looked at how we actually used it, 70% of the traffic was simple lookups by key, with no relationship to anything. What we needed did not exist yet, so we built it and published how it worked.

The paper called it Dynamo, and its ideas travelled far beyond us, shaping a generation of systems that now sit under much of the web. It was the first instance of a pattern I would see repeated for 20 years.

Only pay for what you use

For enterprises, computing meant procurement cycles, contracts, and hardware that took months to arrive and sat idle the moment demand dipped. In 2006 that began to change. You could rent a computer by the hour, call an API, and have a virtual machine running your code minutes later, then shut it down and stop paying when you were done. On-demand infrastructure became the ground much of the modern internet now stands on.

That model came with a cost buried in the architecture. To make renting by the hour work, many customers had to share one physical server, each isolated from the rest, and that isolation ran in software on the very processor the customer was paying for. The networking, the storage access, the monitoring, and the security ran there too, competing for the same cores.

Across the industry, virtualisation carried this tax. On some machines as much as 30% of the compute went to keeping the infrastructure alive rather than running the customer's work.

The virtualisation tax

For a while everyone did what you do when a system is under strain. We tuned the hypervisor, optimised the network path, and clawed back a few points of overhead at a time, but you can only tune your way out of so much.

The deeper problem was that the infrastructure lived in the same place as the customer's code, so every improvement meant touching the processor the customer was paying to use. So we moved it off entirely, onto dedicated hardware that took on all the work that had been stealing those cores.

“Somewhere out there is another assumption we treat as a law of nature, another corner waiting for someone curious enough to invent a way out, another missing piece that will unlock a torrent of innovation. When they find it, hardly anyone will notice that either”

Werner Vogels

We called it Nitro, and the industry has been moving the same direction since. The customer got very nearly the whole server back, and because that work now lived on hardware we controlled, we could encrypt every byte crossing the network at line speed and give an instance a direct path to its storage. The infrastructure finally had room to keep evolving without getting in the customer's way.

This did something else I did not fully appreciate at the time. It gave us a place to put things that had nothing to do with virtualisation, and one of them changed how I think about building distributed systems.

The missing primitive

For my whole career there was one tool every distributed systems engineer was taught never to reach for - the clock. You could not trust time in a distributed system, because perfectly accurate clocks did not exist. There is always some drift, some tiny delay, some error you cannot wish away, and the moment you depend on two machines agreeing on the time, you have built a subtle bug that will surface at the worst possible moment.

Leslie Lamport framed this for a generation of us in the late 1970s, work that earned him a Turing Award. In 1991 Barbara Liskov wrote Practical uses of synchronised clocks in distributed systems, a fine paper describing what trustworthy time could buy you, but the hardware to deliver it did not exist, so the idea sat while our systems grew more elaborate around the gap.

We built vector clocks, distributed locks, leader election, Paxos, two-phase commit, an entire body of machinery whose purpose was to avoid looking at a clock.

As an industry we had poured decades of ingenuity into elaborate ways to live without something, rather than ask whether the absence was really a law of nature. More than 30 years after Liskov's paper, it turned out to be a hardware problem.

We built timing infrastructure whose only job is to deliver accurate, synchronised time from satellites and atomic clocks, passed to purpose-built hardware on the Nitro card, giving every instance a timestamp with a margin of error measured in microseconds.

With time you can actually trust, a whole class of problems falls away. Systems can agree on the order of events without heavy coordination, which lets storage and databases stay consistent across the planet, something many of us had spent years believing was close to impossible. It was a missing primitive, and once it was there an enormous amount of complexity evaporated.

I suspect more of these are hiding in plain sight, assumptions we have built careers around that will look quaint the moment someone supplies the missing piece.

The traits that outlast tools

If there is a thread running through all of this, it is the people. Every few years the ground shifts, and someone asks in earnest whether the machine is about to make them obsolete.

When I went to school I was taught assembler, Cobol, and Pascal, and the industry stopped building on them long ago. My first editor was Vi, then came a slew of integrated development environments (IDEs), then much of the world moved to VS Code, and now developers pair with AI to write code faster than any of us could type it. The tools never stop changing, and adapting to them has always been the job.

So will the machine make you obsolete? Only if you stop evolving.

Less and less of this work is about how well you know a particular language or tool, and more about how deeply you understand the systems you work in and the customer problems you are trying to solve.

There is a parallel to the Renaissance, which arrived after a long stretch of darkness because people grew curious again. Someone worked out the vanishing point, and paintings that had been flat for a thousand years suddenly had depth. The microscope and the telescope made the very small and the very far visible. The printing press put knowledge in the hands of anyone who could read. Art and science became part of the same conversation, and creativity and technology moved forward together.

We are living in another of these moments. Jeff Bezos put it well when he said we sit at the epicentre of several golden ages at once - in AI, in space, in robotics, each accelerating the others.

The people who make the most of it will carry the traits those Renaissance figures did. They stay curious and never stop learning. They break things and learn from what happens. They communicate with precision, and they think in systems, because a change to one service ripples through every service that depends on it. They refuse to accept that the way something has always been done is the way it must be.

The job has always been about high-judgement decisions, taking situations that are complex, ambiguous, and incomplete and finding a way through with creativity and hard-earned experience.

AI will not do that for you. It does not know that the checkout path needs five-nines reliability while an internal dashboard can go dark at peak and no one will care. It cannot hear that a stakeholder who says “make it faster” actually means make it cheaper. In that way little has changed. It is still the most creative job on the planet, where you come in every day and build something from nothing.

The work nobody sees

Most of the work I have done, no one has ever seen, and in that I am not unusual. Someone clicks a button and a package arrives, and they never think about the catalogue, the supply chain, the databases, or the people keeping it all running. They are not supposed to. The clean deployment, the quiet rollback, the outage that never happened because someone planned for it - this is work that succeeds by going unnoticed.

Somewhere out there is another assumption we treat as a law of nature, another corner waiting for someone curious enough to invent a way out, another missing piece that will unlock a torrent of innovation. When they find it, hardly anyone will notice that either.

For 60 years computing has been the steady accumulation of invisible work, each generation laying down a layer the next could stand on and stop thinking about, done well out of pride in doing it properly whether or not anyone was watching. That is the part of the job the tools are never going to touch, and it is the part I want you to hold onto.

Now, go build.

Werner Vogels is chief technology officer at Amazon.

title: Inside Google AI worker’s union drive to instil company ethics
raw_text:
Google DeepMind (GDM) employees are using collective bargaining as a means of “establishing morals” at the company in response to its “material support for Israel’s genocide” in Gaza, but now face “classic union busting” tactics from management.

In May 2026, DeepMind employees launched a unionisation bid to end use of the firm’s technology by Israel and the US military, seeking to be recognised under the United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) union, a national branch of the wider Communication Workers Union (CWU), and Unite the Union.

Computer Weekly has talked with multiple Google DeepMind workers who shared concerns related to the firms’ provision of cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to the Israeli military, which they say have been used to support its genocide against the Palestinian people.

However, Google so far has not responded well to the union effort, with workers telling Computer Weekly that the company has been trying to shut down or sideline internal opposition to the use of its technologies by Israeli authorities.

“Google seems to be rejecting this golden opportunity to genuinely listen to their own staff, the source of all the company’s value, on the fundamental issue of ethics and how those are lived at the company,” said John Chadfield, a CWU national officer for tech workers.

“Googlers don’t want to work for a defence contractor, and they don’t want to only be heard in a superficial way by management. At Google DeepMind, people came to work on things like protein folding, cures for Alzheimer’s, and the detection of cancer. Circling the drain of the military-industrial complex is against everything they want to be involved in."

While tech firms have long collaborated with the Israeli government – which has, for some time, been accused of running an apartheid regime on the Palestinian people – workers said there has been an increasing supply of powerful military and surveillance technologies to Israel since October 2023, including drones, artificial intelligence (AI-)powered targeting systems, cloud computing infrastructure, data analytics tools, biometric databases and high-tech weaponry.

In August 2024, for example, in a recording obtained by +972 Magazine, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) colonel Racheli Dembinsky publicly confirmed for the first time that Google’s cloud and AI services – along with those of Amazon and Microsoft – were being used as part of military operations in Gaza.

Workers said that, in the process of GDM essentially transforming itself into a defence contractor for the Pentagon and IDF, it has become more resistant to transparency and oversight.

“There is no way of monitoring what your work is being used for. Google turned into a defence company like Palantir but pretended to not be as bad,” said one worker, who added that at least if you work for a company like BAE Systems, you know exactly what your work will be used for.

“Google just doesn’t tell you what your work is contributing to. If your work is involved in the commission of war crimes, you could be personally complicit and should know about it as an employee.”

Another worker added that the use of Google’s public cloud storage and processing capabilities by the IDF is a necessary precursor to its AI targeting in Gaza, meaning “Google is in the military kill chain” whether its services are used in direct targeting operations or not.

Workers said that while employee-led efforts to oppose the provision of these technologies to the Israeli government were already underway by January 2025 – including internal petitions sent to company management – their concerns became particularly pressing in the wake of Google’s decision to drop its longstanding pledge to not build AI-powered weapons or surveillance tools a month later in February 2025, culminating in the union drive.

“The petitions just weren’t working so we felt we had to go down the union route,” said one worker, who added that without some sort of legal agreement, it was clear that management could change their mind at any time, even if they had agreed to any demands put forward in the petitions. “They can’t ignore us the same way with the union. We see collective bargaining as a route to establishing a set of morals or values at the company.”

According to another worker, “people [at GDM] were in denial” about the supply of cloud and AI technologies to the IDF – and the purposes they were being used for – until the principles were dropped. They described Google’s decision to jettison its longstanding AI principles as a “watershed moment” for the union effort, highlighting that many employees had joined when the principles were in place.

“The mood changed internally. They were building the tech under those guiding principles, which was then repurposed for things the company explicitly said was out of scope,” they said, adding they were also dropped at a time when more and more was becoming public about Google’s supply of technology to the IDF. “Ethics are complicated, but not when it comes to genocide – something has gone terribly off the rails.”

‘Textbook union busting’

However, multiple workers told Computer Weekly that Google DeepMind has not taken the union push well, employing a range of tactics to shut down or at least discourage participation. The workers said management’s behaviour amounts to “classic union busting”.

This includes “third partying the union”, referring to a common anti-union tactic where employers frame the union as an external, interfering “third party” rather than recognising it as the efforts of the workers themselves.

“The union is cast as undemocratic by DeepMind,” said one worker, who added the firm is attempting to create a “fake separation” between employees and the union. 

Workers said Google DeepMind has also been using its HR department to set up “informal” meetings with employees for breaking its non-solicitation policy, usually for people sending critical messages internally, rather than the formal disciplinary routes available.

According to one worker, this practice is Google DeepMind attempting to avoid formal channels and not put anything in writing, while also attempting to restrict worker organising: “It’s not blatantly illegal, but it’s definitely in a grey area legally.”

In one instance, an AI engineer – who was ultimately dismissed for their further dissemination of flyers and posters internally – was called into a meeting with HR for internally communicating with colleagues about the union effort, where they were “actively discouraged” from making any communications that either criticised the change to Google’s AI principles, or linked the company to Israel’s conduct in Gaza.

“Google fired me for stating the obvious: our work on AI was sold to facilitate genocide,” said the engineer in May 2026, who is not sharing their name at this stage but has made a formal legal claim against the company via a UK employment tribunal.

Despite GDM’s effort to disrupt union organising, however, workers said more and more employees were joining in response to the firms underhanded tactics. As it stands, Computer Weekly has been told that union density is high, with 98% of workers at Google DeepMind backing the formal request for recognition sent to the company in May 2026.

Workers said while they are pursuing a voluntary recognition agreement with the company (which allows for collective bargaining negotiations on a wider remit of topics and issues), they will push for statutory recognition (which limits negotiations to pay, hours of work and holidays) if needs be.

The employees’ letter gave management 10 working days to voluntarily recognise the CWU and Unite as their representatives, or take other steps such as agreeing to mediated negotiations, before a formal legal process is launched to force recognition.

In response, GDM declined to voluntarily recognise the union, but said it would speak to employees about the matter via conversations with mediators present.

However, Computer Weekly has been told by workers that the company were essentially “filibustering us and not wanting to discuss anything real”, and that no one from management with the “potential power to make any meaningful decisions” was in the room for the mediated talks.

“We asked them to put someone from management in the room otherwise there is no point negotiating, but they declined,” said one worker.

Commenting on Google’s anti-union tactics, Chadfield added: “We said from the start that Alphabet management will hand it off to HR administrators as a box-ticking exercise, and that is exactly what they’ve done. Senior management have refused repeated requests to come to the table, and as a result negotiations have made very little progress.”

Computer Weekly contacted Google DeepMind about every aspect of this story.

“We strongly believe our employees should make an informed decision about whether or not to join a union,” said a spokesperson. “We are still in the early stages of the process, have acted in good faith from the outset and continue to engage constructively in unionisation discussions.” 

A spokesperson further claimed that the company does not reprimand employees for expressing their views or engaging in protected union activities, and that while it welcomes open discourse, the company also consistently enforces its workplace guidelines to ensure appropriate use of internal systems.

They added that Google has a large number of public sector cloud customers around the world, and follows a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with its applicable use policies and AI principles.

Previous opposition

The union push at GDM is the latest development in a string of opposition by Google employees to the company’s collaboration with military entities.

For example, Google recently agreed to let the US Department of Defense use its AI models for classified work, a move opposed by more than 600 employees. Google staff worry how the technology will be used given the deal could reportedly open the door to autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of US citizens.

Google employees have also previously protested the ethics of contracts such as Project Nimbus, a joint programme with Amazon to make cloud computing and AI tools available to Israel during its campaign in Gaza.

In July 2025, an investigative report published by Francesca Albanese, the special rapporteur for the “human rights situation in Palestine”, concluded that technology firms globally are actively “aiding and abetting” Israel’s “crimes of apartheid and genocide” against Palestinians.

In particular, she highlighted how the “repression of Palestinians has become progressively automated” by the increasing supply of powerful military and surveillance technologies to Israel, including drones, artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems, cloud computing infrastructure, data analytics tools, biometric databases and high-tech weaponry.

She said that if the companies supplying these technologies had conducted the proper human rights due diligence – including IBM, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Palantir – they would have divested “long ago” from involvement in Israel’s illegal occupation of Gaza and the West Bank.

“After October 2023, long-standing systems of control, exploitation and dispossession metamorphosed into economic, technological and political infrastructures mobilised to inflict mass violence and immense destruction,” she said. “Entities that previously enabled and profited from Palestinian elimination and erasure within the economy of occupation, instead of disengaging are now involved in the economy of genocide.”

title: AWS AI Symposium: TeenTech alumni call for AI literacy in schools
raw_text:
Young people need a “mission in AI [artificial intelligence] literacy” and far more access to extracurriculars that build soft skills if the future workforce is to be ready for AI. They also need adults in the room to mentor, volunteer and sponsor.

That was the call from TeenTech founder Maggie Philbin and two of the charity’s alumni at this week’s AWS Public Sector AI Symposium in London.

Philbin (pictured, left), a former presenter of the BBC’s Tomorrow’s World, founded TeenTech in 2008 to prepare young people for a future “we ourselves don’t fully understand”. She told delegates, “Do not ever underestimate the power that you have to change a young person’s thinking and a young person’s life.”

The skills gap is acute. Research quoted at the event showed 49% of UK organisations cite a skills shortage as their number one barrier to AI adoption, up from 46% last year.

Philbin pointed to the charity’s record. TeenTech runs festivals, company-site events and an award scheme where students develop their own prototypes. Last year, more than 1,700 students completed TeenTech award projects, and more than 1,000 of them were female.

Participation shifts how students see themselves, said Philbin. When they arrive, between 55% and 61% are interested in tech or engineering careers. After the programmes, she said they “not only can see that those opportunities are out there, they believe they could do them and would enjoy them”.

Philbin talked about a student called Charles as a case in point. He was always in detention, she said, and the TeenTech club happened to run in the same room, so a teacher said he might as well join. Mentored by the chief technology officer of Disney, he went on to win straight As at A-level, take a digital apprenticeship with Vodafone and earn a first-class degree.

The effects of promoting technical careers compounds, said Philbin. She pointed to one school in Scotland that reported a 300% increase in students taking STEM subjects and opened an engineering department as a result. Meanwhile, she cited a school in Telford that plans to run the programme across 8,000 students next year. More than 65% of students stay involved for five years or more.

Two alumni on stage closed the session. Miranda (pictured, centre) advocated for teaching AI as “a digital toolkit” rather than something young people “just think of … as a homework” tool. “We need a mission in AI literacy,” she said.

Safa (pictured, right), who switched from a law degree to product design engineering, called for reform. “What we need is for students in secondary school and college level to have more access to extracurriculars that will strengthen their soft skills,” she said. “I think we’d call for education system reform.”

Both women helped shape the Young Person’s Charter for Ethical Innovation, presented at the House of Lords and written, notes Philbin, “entirely in the students’ words”.

She ended with a direct call to action. “Every single person in this room, in some way, could be massively helpful,” said Philbin, urging local government to bring TeenTech to their areas and asking attendees to mentor, volunteer or sponsor.

title: Nationwide consolidates 19 data stores to one in the cloud
raw_text:
Nationwide Building Society has completed a project to cut the number of data stores it uses from 19 to one, using Microsoft technology as part of its integration of Virgin Money.

The use of Microsoft Azure and Azure Databricks will enable the organisation to get more out of its artificial intelligence (AI) investments.

Since chief data and analytics officer Sri Kanisapakkam joined Nationwide in 2023, his team have been working on the challenge, and now complete, there is one “accessible” data platform, according to Nationwide.

“We wanted one unified platform that serves all of the data to the society in one place, on one technology, on the cloud,” he said.

This was critical as the use of AI accelerates. “AI is not magic,” said Kanisapakkam. “It needs to understand how your data is organised and how your data is structured. The data has to be trusted first before you can say your AI is trusted.”

On top of replacing a 45-year-old customer data system, Nationwide, which serves around 19 million members, has already moved 15 million customers off its former core banking engine, and is preparing to integrate around five million Virgin Money customers, according to Paul Ballard, Nationwide’s chief technology officer.

Merger of types

Nationwide’s takeover of Virgin Money, first proposed in 2024, set the wheels in motion for a company that had gone through multiple technology integrations in recent years to integrate into a well-established digital strategy.

Nationwide plotted its future technology in 2008, when it announced an initial £1bn investment in IT to create a foundation for the future. Over the same period, Virgin Money has been through two major acquisitions – with the associated integration projects.

Virgin began life as a basic financial service with Norwich Union, but since acquired Northern Rock for £747m in 2011, and was acquired by Clydesdale and Yorkshire Bank Group for £1.7bn in 2018.

The proposed £2.9bn acquisition of Virgin Money, the biggest banking takeover since 2008, will see Nationwide take on more than 7,000 staff, and create the UK’s second-biggest mortgage and savings company. It will also see the Virgin Money brand disappear over time.

Ballard said the next phase will see the building society work with Microsoft technology to create agents that can talk to its systems.

title: AWS AI Symposium: UHCW adds an operation a day with AI
raw_text:
University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) has added an extra case per daily theatre list, recovered time lost to manual coordination, and exposed a data problem that understated operating theatre utilisation by a fifth. It can also now see theatre activity in real time and act ahead of delays instead of reacting to them.

That’s according to UHCW’s director of operations, Juliet Starkey (pictured, in white), who spoke at this week’s AWS Public Sector AI Symposium in London, where partners Proximie, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Deloitte detailed what they called the largest surgical artificial intelligence (AI) programme the NHS has ever run – real-time surgical intelligence across 104 theatres, endoscopy suites and cath labs, spanning eight hospitals and more than 20,000 procedures a year.

Starkey is director of operations at the Hospital of St Cross in Rugby, part of UHCW, which has worked with Proximie for just over a year. She describes the moment she first saw her own theatre data properly. For one day, it came back from the trust’s own reporting at 66% utilisation, which she knew was wrong. Proximie’s ambient sensors recorded the same list at 88%, beating the NHS benchmark that dictates at least 85% of a planned operating theatre session must be spent on active patient care.

The problem is widespread, according to Proximie, which says about 59% of data entered into electronic patient records carries errors – what Starkey called “garbage in, garbage out” – and that up to 24% of theatre time is recoverable.

Starkey said the technology part was the easy bit. “Change management was absolutely the hardest part,” she said. “You put any technology that has a sensor in and there is a concern that this is about surveillance. And so we had to really drive that this was really about improvement and not about watching individuals.”

The trust took a “crawl, walk, run” approach that started with the plastic surgery team and pain services before expanding. It set up a “task-and-finish” group and held engagement sessions in theatres rather than in boardrooms, so staff could challenge the product.

“Some members of our teams who were, shall we say, apprehensive about this technology coming into theatres are now our biggest advocates,” said Starkey.

Governance mattered as much as buy-in. The trust completed a data protection impact assessment, while Proximie technology obscures images at source so “you can see that there is something on a table, but you can’t make the individual out”. Raw images are not retained, and the productivity data belongs to the trust.

The payoff, said Starkey, is “having that overview of what is happening in our theatres and being able to use that information, that granular-level information to drive change without having to spend hours physically observing what’s happening in the theatres”.

The partnership rests on three legs: Proximie provides the technology, AWS the cloud infrastructure, and Deloitte the change management. “Digital change is never just about the tech,” said Ella O’Regan, who leads Deloitte’s financial and operational improvement work and previously spent 11 years in the NHS. “It’s mainly also about the people.”

Starkey’s definition of a good partner is simple. “A good partner is one that doesn’t just come in and drop technology on you,” she said.

The next step, added Starkey, is to keep the learning spreading from one speciality to others.

title: AWS AI Symposium: Public sector must move to full AI transformation
raw_text:
Public sector organisations must move beyond “conversational AI [artificial intelligence]” to “full transformation”. Those that do, and redesign workflows around advanced AI technology, report average efficiency gains of 68%, against 40% for basic users, with productivity and decision-making improved.

Those are among the messages – and claimed benefits – delegates heard at this week’s AWS Public Sector AI Symposium in London, where Amazon Web Services (AWS) set out its UK investment plans and explained the adoption gap it argues still holds the government back.

Cloud giant AWS reiterated its £8bn commitment to build and operate UK datacentre infrastructure between 2024 and 2028, which it estimates will contribute £14bn to the economy and support 14,000 jobs a year. Amazon already claims a total UK workforce of about 75,000 people.

Research AWS commissioned with Strand Partners found 58% of public sector organisations have adopted AI. Of those, 71% report significant or transformative productivity gains, and 52% say AI has already improved decision-making.

But only 31% have reached the most advanced stage of use – combining multiple models, building custom services, and deploying agentic and autonomous AI – against 24% of all UK businesses. Closing that gap could unlock an estimated £35bn in additional growth by 2030, which AWS likens to the economy of Manchester “sitting on the table waiting”.

David Appel, acting vice-president for worldwide public sector at AWS (pictured), said: “When organisations use AI to redesign workflows, accelerate decision-making, and build entirely new products and services, they report average efficiency gains of 68%, compared with just 40% among basic users.

“We call it production, not preview,” he added. “Not AI as a concept, but AI in action.”

The keynote name-checked AWS-supported production deployments across the public sector. These included: NHS Online, which will let patients receive planned specialist care from a digital NHS trust by the end of 2027; Genomics’ Mystra platform, which lets scientists query genetic data in natural language; surgical intelligence firm Proximie, which claims to recapture nearly a quarter of operating theatre time; and the Ministry of Justice, which used AWS Transform to modernise a legacy application in about 20 hours of developer time rather than an estimated nine-plus months of manual work.

AWS also cited its “sovereign by design” credentials, pointing to its Nitro architecture, and a £15m AI Security Institute alignment project with Amazon and Anthropic.

What the ‘scalers’ do differently

At the AWS event, Hacer Evans, managing director of health and public service lead for Accenture, spoke about the 10% of organisations that genuinely embed AI into core operations, which she dubbed “the scalers”.

She identified four behaviours:

  • Scalers pick a specific value stream and go deep: “They don’t just deploy AI into different parts of the organisation and hope and search for those aggregate gains.” 
  • Scalers treat workforce change as core to the programme, not a side stream. 
  • Scalers prepare a digital core built on “connected data”, “clean integration” and “the right access controls”. 
  • Scalers bake governance in from the start: “They don’t bolt it on once something goes wrong.”

Only 30% of organisations rolling out AI do meaningful upskilling or redeployment alongside it, added Evans, so “the other 70% of organisations are not going to realise the workforce efficiency”.

The final ingredient is leadership. “If you’re delegating understanding downwards, the first thing you have is a leadership gap,” she said. “It is not a technology gap.”

Evans, a former civil servant of 27 years, warns against treating AI as a cost-reduction exercise. The organisations pulling ahead ask “what becomes possible but wasn’t before”, then redesign around the answer – the same leap manufacturers made when they redesigned factories around electricity rather than simply swapping steam engines for motors, she said.

title: Capita meeting self-imposed civil service pension targets ‘not sufficient’, says government
raw_text:
The government said Capita’s performance on the troubled civil service pension scheme “remains unacceptable” despite the outsourcer reporting it has reached its latest target.

In a written update on the disastrous outsourcing contract, Sally Jameson MP, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, said Capita meeting its self-imposed targets is “not sufficient progress” and does not constitute full service recovery.

Although Capita reported meeting its own targets across the “priority” areas of bereavement, death in service, ill health retirement, retirement payments and retirement quotes, the government deemed the overall service levels “unacceptable”.

Earlier this week, Computer Weekly asked Capita about its remediation plan. It said: “We continue to work at pace against the remediation plan submitted to the Cabinet Office. The first milestone fell on 1 September and is subject to review by the Cabinet Office.”

In that review, Cabinet Office minister Jameson said: “Overall performance remains unacceptable, and far too many scheme members continue to face uncertainty while waiting for their cases to be resolved.”

Since it took over the contract from previous supplier MyCSP in December 2025, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises and left claimants in severe financial difficulties. The company has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on Capita, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

Move in-house

In her statement, Jameson reiterated the government’s plan to bring the service in-house. “I will also continue work on actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house.”

Capita also set a target to process cases within key performance indicators from 30 September 2026.

Jameson said there will be a “substantive update” next month following the conclusion of the technical audit and report from the remedial adviser Grant Thornton.

Capita said: “In the meantime, our focus remains on working through outstanding cases and improving the service members receive. Despite the progress made, we recognise the service has not been good enough, particularly for members waiting on bereavement, retirement and quotation cases, and we are sorry for the impact this has had on those members.”

The government’s criticism is shared by people within Capita. Computer Weekly revealed last month that Capita’s CEO, Adolfo Hernandez, was slammed by a staff member after making claims that the “right” things were in place to turn the botched Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) administration around.

Hernandez had written to staff admitting things had not been good enough but that this was being put right: “The service there has not been good enough and we are sorry about the impact on members – but we now have the right people, processes and technology in place to put that right.”

But in a response to Hernandez’s statement, copied to all Capita staff, a member of the pensions team said: “The service provided by Capita surpasses your assertion of ‘not good enough’ – it has been abysmal for members. The fact members have died in waiting due to this whole catastrophe is a really harrowing thought that none of us should have to live with, yet we sadly do.”

The worker said that staff have been trying to air their concerns about the CSPS contract, but that all contacts have been “met with vague, deflective and meaningless responses”.

Jameson’s statement is a sign that the government is getting tough on Capita, a firm that has thrived in the UK public sector.

Capita has a huge UK public sector client base. According to figures from Tussell, Capita currently has 199 public sector contracts worth a combined £7.9bn. Despite the CSPS failures, Capita won the Synergy Business Process Services contract in March, which, according to the official tender, has an estimated value of around £959m over 10 years. The contract supports back-office services for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

title: IBM and NASA make Moon AI model available on Hugging Face
raw_text:
IBM and NASA have published the open NASA‑IBM Lunar Foundation Model on Hugging Face. The pair describe the model as one of the first publicly available foundation models for scientific exploration of the Moon, turning decades of lunar observations into a foundation for discovery, to help scientists surface patterns across data at a scale they claim no single instrument has previously provided.

The model extends an established IBM and NASA collaboration that transforms scientific data into an openly available foundation for discovery for the entire scientific community. 

In 2024, the two organisations created a family of AI foundation models for Earth called Prithvi. These geospatial foundation models were made available on Hugging Face for open science users, startups and enterprises to simplify model training and deployment.

In 2025, IBM and NASA made Surya, the first heliophysics AI foundation model trained on high resolution solar observation data, available on Hugging Face. According to IBM and NASA, this model offers insights into the Sun’s dynamic surface, and can be used to help plan for solar weather that can disrupt technology on Earth and in space.

The latest NASA‑IBM Lunar Foundation Model has been trained on a lunar observation dataset curated by IBM and NASA researchers, which provides multi-instrument data into insights to support the establishment of a sustained human presence on the Moon.

For decades, sensors and instruments have continuously observed the Moon, generating petabytes of data. The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model promises to help researchers accelerate scientific progress by identifying hidden relationships between many different types and resolutions of lunar data.

IBM and NASA said it could be used to investigate multiple lunar phenomena, including potential lunar ice deposits; study lunar volcanic features, called Irregular Mare Patches; and for crater detection.

Permanently shadowed regions are among the Moon’s most difficult environments to observe, but they could contain lunar ice below the surface, which NASA and IBM said indicates the presence of water and oxygen – resources considered essential for a future Moon base and producing rocket fuel for future missions to Mars.

Craters can reveal important clues about the Moon’s history. Crater maps also help NASA select safe landing sites, avoid hazards such as steep slopes and boulders, and plan locations for long-term lunar infrastructure.

“Uncovering the mysteries of the Moon requires an ability to learn from an extraordinary volume of scientific data,” said Juan Bernabe-Moreno, director of IBM Research Europe, UK and Ireland. “The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model gives scientists a foundation to explore the Moon at scale, connecting observations across instruments, revealing patterns that are difficult to see in isolation and providing an open platform the global research community can build on.”

Alongside the model, IBM and NASA scientists have built the first open source lunar dataset of its kind, a unified, machine learning-ready lunar dataset aggregating more than 30 spatially aligned layers from nine instruments across four missions.

The dataset combines tens of thousands of images and maps showing unique geophysical properties of the lunar surface from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and NASA’s Grail (Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory) mission and complementary lunar data from the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Selene (Selenological and Engineering Explorer).
